true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second downsize definition silently overrides the existing width/height API

Lines 145-151 define OptimizedImage.downsize twice: first as downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) and then as downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}). In Ruby the second definition replaces the first, so any existing caller using the four-argument width/height form will now either raise ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments) or have its max_width value interpreted as a complete dimensions string. This is an API/contract break for other thumbnail/downsize callers, not just the new uploads-controller caller.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10 MB client limit ignores configured image and attachment limits

validateUploadedFile previously used Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], which distinguishes images from attachments and respects admin configuration; it now always allows 10 * 1024 KB. If an admin configures a lower limit, the client will accept and upload files the server then rejects (the server-side downsizing only applies to images, so oversized attachments are uploaded in full just to fail), and if an admin configures a higher limit, the client incorrectly blocks valid uploads. The hardcoded value also makes the file_too_large message report 10240 KB regardless of the actual configured limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Percentage downsizing is incompatible with the animated-GIF instructions

The new upload path passes dimensions "80%" with allow_animation taken from SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails. When that setting is true and the file is a GIF, optimize() dispatches to downsize_instructions_animated, which forwards "80%" to resize_instructions_animated as the argument to gifsicle's --resize-fit. --resize-fit expects a WxH geometry, not a percentage scale (gifsicle uses a different option for scaling), so animated GIF downsizing will fail; convert_with returns false, the controller ignores that result, retries the same failing command up to five times, and then proceeds with the still-oversized file.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error handler reports a fabricated 10 MB maximum

In displayErrorForUpload's 413 branch, the message previously used Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb and now always interpolates 10 * 1024 KB as max_size_kb. A 413 is generated by the web server/proxy limit, which is unrelated to this constant, so users will be told the limit is 10 MB even when the proxy or site setting allows far less or more, sending them to retry with files that will continue to fail.

Downsize result is ignored and the loop neither guarantees nor verifies the size limit

The while loop at lines 66-69 calls OptimizedImage.downsize up to five times but discards its boolean return value and performs no check after the loop. If conversion fails, produces a larger file (possible when re-encoding formats such as PNG without a quality/compression change in downsize_instructions), or five 80% reductions are still not enough to get under SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb, create_upload silently continues to Upload.create_for with an oversized/corrupt intermediate file. The feature therefore either fails later with the old size error after expensive retries or stores an upload that does not satisfy the stated invariant.

In-place conversion uses the same path for input and output

OptimizedImage.downsize is called with tempfile.path as both source and destination. The downsize instructions run ImageMagick `convert <file>[0] ... <file>` (and for animated images gifsicle with --output set to the input file), rather than converting to a separate temporary file and atomically replacing the original only on success. Tools that truncate/create the output before fully consuming the input, or that fail part-way, can leave the user's only uploaded copy truncated or corrupted; because the return value is ignored and ensure only closes the tempfile, the corrupted file is then passed to Upload.create_for instead of preserving the original upload.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes on a nil host instead of failing validation

`self.host.sub!(...)` raises NoMethodError when host is nil, e.g. an admin POSTs an embeddable_host with a blank/missing host field from Admin::EmbeddableHostsController. Instead of a 422 validation error via render_json_error, the request 500s. Guard against nil (or use non-mutating sub with to_s) and add a presence validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy raise NoMethodError for a nonexistent host id

`EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` returns nil for an unknown id, and both update (via save_host calling host.host=) and destroy (line 16, host.destroy) then raise NoMethodError, producing a 500 instead of a 404. This is reachable with a stale admin page after a host was deleted in another tab.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration interpolates stored host values directly into SQL and stores them unnormalized

Each legacy host string `h` is interpolated unescaped into the INSERT statement, so a host value containing a single quote breaks the migration and is a SQL-injection vector. Additionally the raw legacy values (which per the old specs may be like 'http://discourse.org' or 'https://example.com/1234') are inserted verbatim, bypassing EmbeddableHost's scheme/path stripping; EmbeddableHost.record_for_host compares lower(host) against the bare URI host, so such migrated rows will never match and embedding for those sites silently breaks after upgrade.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents are swapped between the two fabricator files

category_fabricator.rb now defines only Fabricator(:embeddable_host), while the new embeddable_host_fabricator.rb defines :category, :diff_category, :happy_category and :private_category. Fabrication loads every file so tests still pass, but the swapped names are misleading and invite a future duplicate-definition error when someone adds a fabricator to the file matching its name.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration interpolates stored host values directly into SQL and stores them unnormalized

Each legacy host string `h` is interpolated unescaped into the INSERT statement, so a host value containing a single quote breaks the migration and is a SQL-injection vector. Additionally the raw legacy values (which per the old specs may be like 'http://discourse.org' or 'https://example.com/1234') are inserted verbatim, bypassing EmbeddableHost's scheme/path stripping; EmbeddableHost.record_for_host compares lower(host) against the bare URI host, so such migrated rows will never match and embedding for those sites silently breaks after upgrade.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when embed_category site setting is absent

Site settings are only persisted in site_settings when overridden, so most installs have no 'embed_category' row. `execute(...)[0]` is then nil and `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError, aborting the migration (and deployment). The fallback on line 15 has the same problem for 'uncategorized_category_id'. The lookups must handle an empty result set.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

false_positives.candidate:
No uniqueness constraint on host allows duplicate hosts with conflicting categories

There is no uniqueness validation on host and the migration creates no unique index. Admins can create two rows for the same host pointing at different categories; record_for_host then returns whichever row the database happens to return first, so embedded topics are filed into an unpredictable category and host_allowed?/category selection becomes nondeterministic.

edit action crashes when the host has no resolvable category

`this.get('host.category.id')` throws if host.category is undefined. That happens for a host whose category was deleted, and also after save() sets `host.category` to Discourse.Category.findById(categoryId) which is undefined when no category was chosen (the server silently substitutes the uncategorized category, which the client does not mirror). Clicking Edit then breaks the admin page; use a safe get (host.category && host.category.id) and sync the category returned by the server.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser row

TopicUser.find_by can return nil for a logged-in user who has never visited, posted in, or otherwise interacted with the topic (for example, opening the unsubscribe URL directly or after the row was removed). The next line calls tu.notification_level on nil, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500 instead of unsubscribing. The action should create/update the record through the existing TopicUser.change mechanism (as set_notifications does) so a missing row is created with the muted/regular level.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
Direct TopicUser save bypasses notification-change bookkeeping and leaves stale state

Mutating tu.notification_level and calling tu.save! bypasses TopicUser.change, which is the established path used by set_notifications: it stamps notifications_changed_at, sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed, runs observe_after_save_callbacks_for, and publishes a MessageBus /topic/:id notification_level_change event. Because @topic_view was also built before the mutation, the rendered/serialized response and any already-open client can keep showing the old watching/tracking level even though the database changed, and downstream observers never learn of the change. Use TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...) instead.

Emails with add_unsubscribe_link but no topic unsubscribe_url now raise

The server locale string unsubscribe_link now interpolates %{unsubscribe_url}, and both body (line 90) and html_part (line 67) call I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args) whenever add_unsubscribe_link is true. MessageBuilder is generic: any caller that sets add_unsubscribe_link without also passing unsubscribe_url (previously valid, and the behaviour the existing specs exercised before they were edited to pass a URL) will now raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument and fail to deliver the email instead of falling back to the plain user-preferences unsubscribe text. The per-topic sentence should only be appended when unsubscribe_url is present.

No test covers the new unsubscribe behaviour end-to-end

The only spec change passes unsubscribe_url into an existing builder fixture but adds no assertion that the topic unsubscribe URL appears in the text body or HTML part, and there are no controller specs for TopicsController#unsubscribe at all (level transitions watching/tracking->regular and regular->muted, missing TopicUser row, wrong slug redirect, JSON vs HTML). The core state-transition logic of this feature can regress or crash without any test failing.

State-changing unsubscribe is performed by a plain GET request

The new server route is GET t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe and this action immediately mutates notification_level and saves it. Email security scanners, link prefetchers, browser pre-rendering, or a third party tricking a logged-in user into loading the URL (CSRF via GET, which Rails forgery protection does not cover) will unsubscribe/mute the user without any intentional click or confirmation. The GET should only render a confirmation page and the mutation should require a non-GET request, as the Ember notification dropdown already can perform.

topicUnsubscribe route is shadowed by topic.fromParamsNear

The topic resource defined just above already has a child route fromParamsNear with path '/:nearPost', i.e. /t/:slug/:id/:nearPost, which matches the literal segment 'unsubscribe'. Ember's router recognises routes in definition order, so /t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe is matched as the normal topic page with nearPost='unsubscribe' before the later top-level topicUnsubscribe route is considered; the unsubscribe template/controller therefore never renders on a full page load or transition. The unsubscribe route needs to be defined so it wins recognition over the :nearPost wildcard (or handled inside the topic route).

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write and mutates state during validation

should_block? is called from EmailValidator.validate_each, i.e. during model validation, yet it increments match_count/last_match_at with a non-atomic read-modify-write save. Two consequences: (1) concurrent registration attempts with the same blocked email lose increments (both read the same match_count and write the same +1 value) — use an atomic update such as update_all('match_count = match_count + 1'); (2) a single signup attempt validates twice (UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, which re-validates), and attempts rejected for unrelated reasons also persist a count, so match_count does not reflect actual blocked attempts. The counter update should be atomic and ideally separated from the pure predicate.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and can be bypassed by changing letter case

should_block? does an exact database string match on the supplied email, and neither BlockedEmail nor EmailValidator normalizes case (or surrounding whitespace) before lookup/storage. Email addresses are treated case-insensitively elsewhere (e.g. User.email_hash downcases), so a blocked address such as bad@spamclub.com can register as Bad@Spamclub.com and evade the block. Normalize emails to a canonical form (strip + downcase) on BlockedEmail save and in should_block? before querying.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
action_type is not validated against BlockedEmail.actions

The model validates only presence/uniqueness of email. Any integer (or a typo'd value inserted via console/import) is accepted for the NOT NULL action_type column, and should_block? treats every value other than actions[:block] as non-blocking, so a malformed block entry silently fails open instead of surfacing an error. Add an inclusion validation over BlockedEmail.actions.values for action_type.

rejectedEmails is a mutable array defined on the controller prototype and shared by all instances

rejectedEmails: Em.A([]) is defined in the object passed to Discourse.Controller.extend, so the same array instance lives on the prototype and is shared across every instance of the controller rather than being per-instance state. pushObject in createAccount therefore leaks rejected addresses across controller instances / modal lifecycles for the whole page session, permanently flagging an address as invalid client-side even in a fresh signup attempt. Initialize the array in init (or set it when the modal opens) instead of on the prototype.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring matching instead of origin equality

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` accepts any e.origin that happens to be a substring of discourseUrl, rather than requiring e.origin to equal the Discourse origin (scheme + host + port, with trailing slash stripped). Shortened/prefix origins therefore pass, weakening the check that is supposed to ensure only the Discourse iframe can resize the embed. Compare the normalized origin exactly instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped referer interpolated into JavaScript and used as postMessage targetOrigin

`'<%= request.referer %>'` inserts the Referer header into a single-quoted JS string with no JavaScript/HTML escaping. A referer containing a quote or `</script>` breaks out of the string/script context and executes attacker JS in the Discourse origin inside the embed iframe. Additionally, postMessage's targetOrigin must be a serialized origin (scheme/host/port), not a full URL with a path; passing the full referer will cause browsers to drop the resize message, so legitimate resizing also fails.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
import mutates caller's contents string and interpolates unescaped URL into HTML

`contents << "...#{url}..."` mutates the string passed by the caller (raising FrozenError for frozen literals and corrupting reused strings, e.g. feed item content reused on retry), and the URL is interpolated unescaped into a single-quoted href attribute. A URL containing a quote can break out of the attribute and inject markup into the raw-HTML post. Duplicate the contents string first and HTML-escape/attribute-escape the URL when building the imported-from link.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed crashes on feed items without content and one bad item aborts the whole import

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` raises NoMethodError when an RSS/Atom item has no content element (common for summary-only feeds; SimpleRSS may return nil or a different field such as description/summary). Because there is no per-item rescue, the exception aborts poll_feed mid-loop, so all remaining items are never imported and the hourly job fails on every run for such a feed. Guard nil content (fall back to description/summary) and isolate failures per item.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped referer interpolated into JavaScript and used as postMessage targetOrigin

`'<%= request.referer %>'` inserts the Referer header into a single-quoted JS string with no JavaScript/HTML escaping. A referer containing a quote or `</script>` breaks out of the string/script context and executes attacker JS in the Discourse origin inside the embed iframe. Additionally, postMessage's targetOrigin must be a serialized origin (scheme/host/port), not a full URL with a path; passing the full referer will cause browsers to drop the resize message, so legitimate resizing also fails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

false_positives.candidate:
Disqus import silently drops the --category option and now requires fetching each thread URL

The change removes the documented `method_option :category` (breaking existing invocations that pass -c, which Thor will now reject/ignore) and replaces local PostCreator creation with TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], ...), which performs a live HTTP fetch of each Disqus thread link. If a link is dead, redirects, or the site is offline, post becomes nil and all comments for that thread are silently skipped, whereas previously the topic was created locally from the export data. Preserve category support or document its removal, and fall back to creating the topic from export data when the remote fetch fails.

Raw-HTML posts bypass all sanitization, enabling stored XSS from feeds/remote pages

Post#cook returns `raw` verbatim when cook_method is raw_html, and TopicEmbed.import creates such posts from untrusted RSS/Atom content (Jobs::PollFeed) and arbitrary remote-page content extracted by Readability (TopicEmbed.import_remote). Neither path sanitizes script tags, event-handler attributes, or javascript: URLs before storage, and views output post.cooked (e.g. embed/best.html.erb uses `raw post.cooked`, and normal topic views trust cooked HTML). A malicious or compromised feed/page on the embeddable host therefore stores active HTML/JS that executes in the Discourse origin for every reader, not only in the embed iframe.

Spec expects TopicRetriever in controller but implementation enqueues Jobs::RetrieveTopic

The 'tells the topic retriever to work' example stubs/expects TopicRetriever.new and retriever.retrieve, but EmbedController#best at app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:15 instead calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...). TopicRetriever is never referenced by the controller, so this expectation fails (Jobs.enqueue is not stubbed and may enqueue a real job). The test as shipped does not pass against the implementation and does not verify the RetrieveTopic job arguments; update it to expect Jobs.enqueue with user_id/embed_url.

import_remote fetches arbitrary URLs server-side with open() and no timeout/validation

TopicEmbed.import_remote does `open(url).read` on a URL ultimately derived from the user-supplied embed_url parameter (EmbedController -> Jobs::RetrieveTopic -> TopicRetriever). TopicRetriever only compares URI host to embeddable_host; there is no timeout, size limit, scheme validation inside import itself, or protection against redirects to internal addresses (open-uri follows redirects). A URL on the allowed host that redirects to an internal/metadata endpoint, or a slow/huge response, can be used for SSRF or to tie up Sidekiq workers. Validate the final URL, set open/read timeouts, and cap response size.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items() omits the -moz-box alignment counterpart it claims to support

`flexbox()` emits `display: -moz-box` for legacy Firefox, but `align-items()` provides no `-moz-box-align`, so the vertical alignment supplied here (e.g. `center` for `.d-header .contents` and `.small-action`, `baseline` for bullet badges) silently does not apply in the very legacy-Firefox layout mode the mixin set targets, leaving those rows top-aligned there. Also note `-ms-align-items` on line 121 is not a real IE10 property (IE10 uses `-ms-flex-align`), so it is dead code. Add `-moz-box-align: $alignment;` (and remove/ignore the bogus -ms line) for consistent coverage.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() mixin is off by one for legacy box layout

The mixin emits the supplied value unchanged for both modern `order` and legacy `-webkit-box-ordinal-group`/`-moz-box-ordinal-group`, but the legacy properties are 1-based while `order` is 0-based (legacy default is 1, modern default is 0). Thus `order(2)` on .extra-info-wrapper and `order(3)` on .panel behave as ordinal-groups 2/3 in old WebKit/Firefox versus orders 2/3 in modern browsers, and any future `order(0)` would be invalid and `order(1)` would collide with unordered items in legacy browsers. The legacy declarations should use `$val + 1` so both models produce the same ordering.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.

false_positives.candidate:
Flex conversion strands .small-action button next to the text instead of at the right edge

`.small-action` is now `display: flex` (line 264), so its children become flex items and the `float: right` on its `button` (line 309) is ignored per the flexbox spec. Previously the float pinned the button (e.g. the dismiss/close control) to the right side of the row; now, with no `margin-left: auto`, `justify-content`, or explicit `order`/alignment on the button, it will sit immediately after `.small-action-desc` on the left. Add `margin-left: auto` to the button (and drop the dead float) to preserve the right-aligned placement.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the question mark and will never be used

The serializer defines `def include_website_name` without the trailing `?`, while every other inclusion predicate in this file (e.g. include_email?, include_card_image_badge_id?) and the ActiveModel::Serializer convention require `include_website_name?`. As a result the `website.present?` guard is dead code and `website_name` is serialized even when the user has no website, emitting `website_name: null` in the API payload instead of omitting the attribute.

false_positives.candidate:
Sibling-subdomain branch of website_name has no test coverage

The second branch (lines 144-146) implements distinct logic for sibling subdomains such as www.example.com versus forum.example.com, stripping the first DNS label before comparing. The new specs in spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb only cover unrelated domains, identical domains, and a parent-domain website; none exercise this equal-length, >2-label branch, so a regression in the label-stripping comparison would ship undetected.

website_name bypasses the untrusted-attribute restriction for TL0 users viewed anonymously

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes`, so it is hidden from anonymous viewers when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` applies (TL0 users), but the newly added `website_name` attribute is not added to that list. `website_name` is derived directly from the website URL (host, and in the same-domain case host plus full path), so anonymous visitors can still learn a TL0 user's website host/path from `website_name` even though `website` itself is suppressed, defeating the anti-spam/privacy restriction.

website_name drops query string and shows a trailing slash for root URLs

When the domains match, the method returns `website_host + URI(website).path` only. For a website such as `http://example.com/user?tab=posts` the displayed name silently loses `?tab=posts` despite the feature claiming to show the complete URL path, and for `http://example.com/` it returns `example.com/` instead of the bare host that the old client-side `website.split('/')[2]` produced.

true_positives.golden_comment: In .topic-meta-data h5 a, the original code had color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%) but was changed to dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%)). The lightness for the light theme changed from 30% to 70%, which is a dramatic inversion
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embedded-post author link swaps the light and dark lightness values

This rule originally used scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%). The change writes dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%)), so the light-theme argument is 70% instead of the original 30% and the dark-theme argument is 30% instead of the complementary 70%. Light-theme embedded-post author links become much lighter than before and dark-theme links do not get the intended lightened secondary color. It should be dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%)).

Consider reviewing this (also applies to a similar .name change in the mobile variant).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

false_positives.candidate:
Group creation silently ignores the alias_level sent by the client

The client's Group.asJSON() sends name, alias_level and visible on POST /admin/groups, but create only assigns name and visible. A non-default alias level chosen in the admin form for a new group is silently discarded and the model default is used instead; update handles alias_level, so create should assign params[:alias_level] the same way.

Members endpoint accepts unbounded, zero or negative limit/offset

limit and offset are taken from params with only to_i and no clamping. A request such as members.json?limit=1000000 forces serializing that many users in one response (memory/CPU/DoS risk), while limit=0 is echoed back in meta.limit and makes the admin client's totalPages/currentPage divide by zero, and negative values go straight into SQL limit/offset. Clamp limit to a sane range (e.g. 1..200) and offset to >= 0.

Public group members page now silently truncates to the first 50 members

members now always applies limit (default 50) and offset, but the public discourse/templates/group/members.hbs view and discourse/routes/group-members.js.es6 route add no pagination controls or further fetching. Previously non-automatic groups returned all members and automatic groups up to 200. Groups with more than 50 members will now show only the first 50 on the public members page with no way to reach the rest.

Remove-member link visibility checks `automatic` on the wrong context

This template is rendered per member via {{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}, so its context is the member (a Discourse.User), which has no `automatic` property. {{#unless automatic}} therefore always renders the remove link, including for automatic groups whose members the server refuses to remove (422 from can_not_modify_automatic). The check needs the group's automatic flag, not the member's.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Cached translations can permanently cache a missing-translation result before fallback locales are loaded

translate() caches translate_no_cache(key) in the LRU under only key+locale+backend, but with fallbacks the result depends on whether the site-default and :en locale files have been loaded yet. If a key is first translated in the user locale before its fallback locales are loaded, I18n returns a 'translation missing' string and that string is frozen and cached; loading the fallback locale afterwards does not clear @cache (only reload! does), so users can keep seeing missing-translation text until restart/reload. The cache must be invalidated when load_locale loads a new locale, or translations must ensure all fallback locales are loaded before caching.

Fallback locales are only ensured loaded for web requests

I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! is called only from ApplicationController#set_locale. Background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, and other code paths that set I18n.locale without going through this controller will translate with only config.locale loaded (translate_accelerator only auto-loads config.locale), so fallback lookups against the site default/:en can return missing translations instead of the English/site text. Move the ensure-loaded logic into the I18n translation/load path itself (or into every locale-setting entry point), not just the request cycle.

FallbackLocaleList is a Hash in name only and drops configured fallback semantics

I18n.fallbacks is normally an I18n::Locale::Fallbacks object that supports defaults, explicit per-locale mappings, and locale expansion (e.g. en_US -> en). Replacing it with a Hash subclass whose [] ignores any stored entries and always fabricates [locale, site_default, :en] means code or gems that assign/inspect fallbacks (I18n.fallbacks[:de] = [...], defaults, include?) silently lose those settings, and regional locales get no parent-language fallback (zh_TW never falls back to zh, pt_BR never to pt). Implement the fallback object API or subclass I18n::Locale::Fallbacks and override compute instead of faking a Hash.

SiteSetting is consulted on every fallback translation lookup

FallbackLocaleList#[] calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym every time I18n asks for the fallback chain, which happens during translation lookups rather than once per request. This adds a site-setting lookup (and potential cache/database work) to hot translation paths and also makes translation depend on SiteSetting being available; if default_locale is nil/blank during boot, migrations, or in a bare console/job context, to_sym on nil (or loading a blank locale) can break otherwise-valid translations. Compute/cache the site default safely (e.g. per request or with a nil/blank guard) instead of querying it inside the fallback map.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset queryset slicing raises AssertionError, not graceful pagination

When enable_advanced_features is true and a user supplies a cursor with a negative offset (Cursor.from_string accepts e.g. '0:-100:0'), this branch does queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset<0. Django QuerySets explicitly raise AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported, contrary to the comment claiming the ORM handles it automatically. Any superuser/global-access user can craft ?optimized_pagination=true&cursor=... to reliably 500 the audit-log endpoint, and stop can also become <=0 giving meaningless slices. Negative offsets must be rejected/clamped with BadPaginationError as OffsetPaginator/ChainPaginator do.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator uses numeric key handling for a datetime ordering

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does int(math.floor(value)) on getattr(item, self.key) and value_from_cursor returns cursor.value unchanged. The only caller, OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, orders by '-datetime', so value is a datetime: math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError when build_cursor computes next/prev cursors, making the optimized path return 500 on any non-empty page. Even if it did not crash, value_from_cursor would pass a raw integer timestamp into build_queryset's datetime comparison instead of converting it with DateTimePaginator's multiplier/fromtimestamp logic, producing wrong filtering. The paginator should reuse DateTimePaginator's key conversion or the endpoint should not use it for -datetime.

The shared BasePaginator.get_result now clamps negative offsets only when not cursor.is_prev; for is_prev cursors it passes the raw user-controlled offset to queryset[start_offset:stop]. true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
organization_context.member may be None

enable_advanced is computed as request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access. For non-superuser requests where the organization context has no member (e.g. superuser-less API/token contexts that reach this endpoint, or members not yet resolved), evaluating .has_global_access on None raises AttributeError and 500s a previously working endpoint; the check is evaluated on every request, not only when optimized_pagination=true, because Python evaluates the right-hand side regardless of use_optimized's value only gated by the boolean expression order — actually enable_advanced is always computed before the if, so all non-superuser requests without a member regress.

false_positives.candidate:
Flush-time max_segment_spans guard removed with no equivalent for non-Lua growth

_load_segment_data no longer enforces max_segment_spans (the metric/log/skip branch was deleted). The only remaining cap is the Lua insert path, which does not cover segments already stored as sets, keys built by the initial batched ZADD before per-span Lua runs interleaved with other batches, or future writers. Oversized segments can now be loaded and produced downstream unbounded by span count, reintroducing the memory/downstream-size risk the guard existed for.

Insert-time eviction silently discards earliest-ending spans from segments

Once a merged set exceeds a hardcoded 1000 members, zpopmin removes the lowest-scored members, where the score is now end_timestamp_precise. This silently deletes arbitrary child spans (those ending earliest) from a segment that will later be flushed as if complete, with no metric, log, or segment-too-large outcome as the previous flush-time check produced. It corrupts segment data rather than rejecting/skipping oversized segments, and the hardcoded 1000 also ignores SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001) and any configured value.

Redirect chain traversal cut from 10000 to 1000 breaks deep segment trees

The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects to find the canonical set for a span now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000, and the comment explaining that deeper trees may not join correctly was removed. Segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects will resolve set_span_id to an intermediate span, so spans are split into multiple segments (flushed separately with wrong segment_id/is_segment attribution) — a silent correctness regression for deep traces that previously worked.

Required end_timestamp_precise turns malformed/legacy spans into poison pills

process_batch now does val['end_timestamp_precise'] with direct indexing for every message. Any span payload lacking that field (older producers, partial/relay variants the previous code tolerated since it never read the field) raises KeyError inside the batch function, failing the whole batch and causing redelivery of the same poison message indefinitely. The new Span field in buffer.py is also a required positional-or-keyword argument added before the defaulted is_segment_span, breaking any other Span(...) construction sites that don't pass it.

SET-to-ZSET conversion breaks in-flight Redis segments during deployment

Existing span-buf:s:* keys in Redis are regular sets created by SADD. The new code unconditionally issues ZADD in process_spans, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN in add-buffer.lua, and ZSCAN in _load_segment_data against those same key names. Redis returns WRONGTYPE for these commands on set-typed keys, so during rollout every trace with an unflushed segment (up to redis_ttl=3600s old) errors in the consumer pipeline instead of being flushed; there is no key versioning, type check, or migration/drain step.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key compresses project IDs into a single hash value

Eligibility is cached under hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))) rather than the project IDs themselves. Different project sets whose tuple hash collides share one cached allowlist verdict for 60s, so a non-allowlisted set can be treated as allowlisted (or vice versa) and counts are silently weighted/unweighted incorrectly. invalidate_upsampling_cache repeats the same scheme and cannot disambiguate. Build the key from the joined sorted IDs instead of a lossy hash.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset

_get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset, which get_event_stats_factory may replace (e.g. dashboard discover-split passes split_dataset=discover or the original scoped dataset), but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` instead. The transform decision therefore does not describe the dataset actually queried: split/error queries can miss upsampling and transaction-like split queries can be transformed based on the wrong dataset, producing wrong counts or invalid sample_weight queries.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental gitlink file added to the repository root

The PR adds a new root entry 'sentry-repo' containing 'Subproject commit a5d2909...', i.e. an accidental nested-repo gitlink rather than application code. Merging it creates a stray submodule-like entry without .gitmodules metadata, which breaks/clutters checkouts and tooling; it should be removed from the change.

Substring check treats negated/non-error queries as error-focused

_is_error_focused_query returns True whenever the raw query text contains 'event.type:error', including '!event.type:error' (explicitly excluding errors), quoted/tag values containing that text, or a broader OR query that also includes transactions. For Discover this incorrectly rewrites count() to sum(sample_weight) for transaction/non-error results, yielding wrong totals or queries against rows without meaningful sample_weight. The parsed query conditions, not a substring search, need to establish that results are errors only.

sum(sample_weight) undercounts events whose sample_weight is NULL

The aggregate is sum(sample_weight) with no coalesce/fallback. Events stored before client error sampling was populated, or events without a sample rate, can have NULL sample_weight; ClickHouse sum ignores NULLs, so those events contribute 0 instead of 1. Once any allowlisted project is queried, historical/unsampled errors silently disappear from count() results instead of counting with weight 1 (e.g. sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))).

upsampled_count is enabled for the errors dataset but only registered in Discover

_should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True unconditionally for sentry.snuba.errors, so count() is rewritten to upsampled_count() for dataset=errors requests. The new SnQLFunction is only added to Discover's function_converter in src/sentry/search/events/datasets/discover.py; the errors dataset has its own function converter and does not gain this function from that change. Errors-dataset timeseries requests for allowlisted projects will fail function resolution instead of returning upsampled counts.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public user-callable function

Unlike the internal count helpers around it, the new SnQLFunction is not marked private=True. Any user can therefore send yAxis=upsampled_count() directly on any Discover query/project, bypassing the endpoint's all-projects-allowlisted and error-only checks. On transaction queries this can fail on sample_weight or return misleading weighted counts; the function should be private so only the server-side rewrite can invoke it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error events can be paired with the wrong nodestore payload

`fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids` but then pairs them with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a mapping keyed by node id, not a sequence guaranteed to align positionally with `error_ids`; if an event is missing or the mapping order differs, an error ID is combined with another event's title/message/timestamp (the `if data is not None` check does not fix mis-pairing). This corrupts the chronological error context sent to Seer. Look up each payload by its generated node id instead of zipping values.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.

It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mixed age/timestamp validation misses falsy-but-present values

`validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` check `self.initial_data.get("age")` / `get("timestamp")` for truthiness. A report containing `timestamp` plus `age: 0` (a valid, present age) passes validation because `0` is falsy, violating the serializer's own rule that the two fields must not coexist and letting ambiguous Working-Draft/Editor's-Draft reports through. Presence should be tested with `is not None` / `in` rather than truthiness.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Assemble analytics are recorded for rejected and feature-disabled requests

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before request-body validation, so 404 feature-disabled responses and 400 invalid requests are counted as assemble events. This inflates adoption/usage metrics with requests that never assembled an artifact. The event should be recorded only after the feature gate (and ideally after validation succeeds), or carry a field distinguishing rejected requests.

Hidden span attributes are only hidden while searching

With no search text the function returns `sortAttributes(attributes)` unfiltered, so the supposedly hidden attributes are still displayed by default and only disappear after the user types a query. true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code comparison is case-sensitive and only strips dashes

This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reschedule path bypasses the deferred-cancellation fix and leaks the reminder row

For a rescheduled booking this calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true). With immediateDelete=true that function (emailReminderManager.ts lines 213-223) immediately POSTs a SendGrid 'cancel' for the batch and returns without deleting the WorkflowReminder row and without setting cancelled=true. false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
One failing SendGrid cancellation blocks all other cancellations

The whole cancellation loop is wrapped in a single try/catch and every SendGrid request is awaited inside the loop. If one request fails (e.g. an invalid/empty batch_id for a reminder that was marked scheduled without an actual mail, a SendGrid 400, or a transient error), execution jumps to the catch, the queued Prisma deletes in workflowRemindersToDelete are never awaited/executed, and none of the remaining reminders in remindersToCancel are cancelled. The same failing reminder is returned by findMany on every subsequent cron run, so it can permanently poison the batch and cancelled emails for other bookings continue to be sent. Each reminder should be cancelled/deleted in its own try/catch.

Reminders cancelled shortly before send time can still be delivered between cron runs

Cancellation now only takes effect when this cron next runs and finds cancelled=true with scheduledDate <= now+1h. If a booking is cancelled after the last cron run before the reminder's scheduledDate (the PR description states the cron runs every 15 minutes), SendGrid delivers the email at scheduledDate before any subsequent cron invocation can POST the cancel. The previous code cancelled the batch synchronously at booking-cancellation time; the new design reintroduces a send window for all cancellations made within one cron interval of the send time, so 'cancelled booking' reminders will still occasionally be sent. An immediate cancel is needed for reminders whose scheduledDate is before the next expected cron run.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Calendar/video deletions are fire-and-forget and outside the try/catch

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` discards the promises returned by the async callback. The surrounding try/catch (lines 124-139) therefore cannot catch errors from `await getCalendar(...)` or `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting`, and `Reschedule` can return and send the reschedule email before the old calendar/video events are deleted, leaving orphaned events; on serverless runtimes the deletions may never run at all. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are eagerly executed for every app

All `import(...)` expressions are evaluated immediately when the `appStore` object literal is constructed, so importing `appStore` starts loading all 29 app modules regardless of which app is actually needed. This defeats the stated lazy/async-import purpose, retains the startup/bundle-loading cost for every consumer, and creates promises for unused apps whose rejection (e.g. a broken optional app) would be an unhandled rejection since nothing ever awaits that entry. Imports should only be initiated on access, e.g. via factory functions `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")` with callers awaiting the factory.

Recurring-booking calendar deletions race with apiDeletes consumption

In the recurring-cancellation branch, deletions are pushed into `apiDeletes` from inside a `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` callback. Because `getCalendar` is now async, none of these pushes happen synchronously, so the later `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 (and the `await apiDeletes` at line 617) typically snapshot an empty/incomplete array. The handler can finish and the process can terminate before the external calendar events are deleted. Await the per-credential work with `Promise.all`/`for...of` and push the deletion promises before they are consumed.

requestReschedule deletions are not awaited before mutation completes

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` discards all returned promises. The mutation proceeds immediately to send the reschedule email and webhooks and returns while deletions are still pending (and any failure becomes an unhandled rejection), so the old calendar/video event can survive a successful reschedule response. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`.

dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...) compares two distinct Dayjs objects with ===, which is always false, so the intended zero-length override (whole day unavailable) branch is dead. The PR description claims fixed hosts' date overrides are now honoured for round-robin events, but the only added test re-queries the existing personal-event date-override scenario in Asia/Dhaka and expects identical UTC slots. When a slot is on a date-override day and inside the override window, the find callback returns nothing, dateOverrideExist is true, and checkIfIsAvailable returns true at line 134 without reaching the busy.every() check at the bottom. true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung flusher processes are never killed before replacement

Processes are created with multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose SpawnProcess class is not an instance of multiprocessing.Process (the default-context Process class) on Linux. The isinstance check therefore skips process.kill() for a hung flusher, after which _create_process_for_shards starts a replacement for the same shards. The hung and replacement processes can then concurrently flush the same Redis shards, racing flush/done_flush and potentially producing duplicate segments or interfering with each other's in-progress flushes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes accepts zero and negative values without validation

The new click option accepts any int. A negative value flows to SpanFlusher where min(negative, len(assigned_shards)) yields a negative num_processes and range() produces no processes at all: spans are written to Redis and offsets committed but nothing ever flushes them, with no error. A direct flusher_processes=0 via the factory is instead silently converted by `max_processes or len(...)` to one process per shard, the opposite of the requested limit. The option/factory should reject values < 1.

Flusher processes are not terminated in join() due to the same isinstance check

As in the restart path, join() only calls process.terminate() when isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is true, which is false for SpawnProcess objects created from the spawn context on Linux. join() can therefore return while flusher processes are still running after the deadline; a subsequent rebalance/strategy for the same shards can run concurrently with these orphaned (until parent exit) flushers and duplicate work.

Multi-process flusher test never verifies any segment is flushed

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts process counts and shard distribution, then joins; it submits no spans and asserts no produced output. The threaded produce_to_pipe path with multiple shards sharing processes, per-process restart/health bookkeeping, and the spawn-process path used in production are all unexercised, so regressions that drop or duplicate segments when shards share a flusher (or when a flusher restarts) would pass CI.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Commit scan is O(offset window) every second

get_committable_offsets() runs every 1s in _commit_loop and, per partition, iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)`, i.e. over the entire uncommitted offset window, allocating/scanning proportionally to backlog size. Combined with the unbounded queues, a large backlog (exactly the slow-item scenario this mode targets) makes each commit tick O(window) per partition and can consume a full thread/CPU while commits fall further behind. Tracking only the contiguous head (e.g. sorted outstanding minimum) would be O(1)/O(log n).

Final offsets are never committed on close and closed pool is reused after rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown(), so any items drained/completed during pool shutdown are completed after the last _commit_loop iteration and are never passed to commit_function. Worse, the queue_pool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory and the same pool is passed to every strategy from create_with_partitions(); close() shuts its queues down irreversibly (queue.shutdown()), so after an Arroyo partition rebalance/revocation the factory creates a new strategy backed by a dead pool. Subsequent FixedQueuePool.submit() puts raise queue.ShutDown, which SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches and then add_offset+complete_offset, causing offsets to be committed without the results ever being processed.

Group-to-queue assignment uses randomized hash()

get_queue_for_group() uses Python's built-in hash() on a str, which is randomized per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, despite the docstring calling it 'consistent hashing'. The mapping differs across consumer processes/restarts, so the same subscription is not consistently assigned as documented and distribution cannot be reasoned about or reproduced in tests/operations; within a fleet this also gives no stable sharding guarantee. Use a stable digest (e.g. hashlib/md5 already used elsewhere for grouping) modulo num_queues.

OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition revocation

OffsetTracker keeps all_offsets/outstanding/last_committed/partition_locks forever and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy exposes no revocation/flush hook to clear a partition. If a partition is revoked and later reassigned (possibly at an offset <= the previously recorded last_committed, e.g. after a rebalance or offset reset), get_committable_offsets() starts at last_committed+1 and can never emit a commit until processing passes the stale high-water mark, so processed results go uncommitted and are redelivered; removed partitions also leak sets/locks for the life of the factory-owned pool.

Shutdown abandons queued work items

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True for every worker before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() only checks `while not self.shutdown` at the top of its loop, so a worker that finishes its current item exits immediately even if its queue still contains pending items, and a worker blocked in get() that returns an item may process at most one more. The remaining queued items are therefore never processed and their offsets never complete, contrary to the immediate=False drain semantics. On consumer shutdown/rebalance those messages must be redelivered (or are lost if later code marks them complete), defeating the claimed graceful shutdown.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize and submit() does an unconditional put(). The class/strategy docstrings claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing ever blocks or rejects: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() is called by Arroyo for every polled message and will enqueue indefinitely if one subscription/queue is slow, growing memory unboundedly, holding WorkItem/message references, and building a huge outstanding-offset window that can stall commits and trigger max.poll.interval rebalances. A bounded queue (with blocking or Arroyo-appropriate rejection) is required.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key uses ambiguous underscore concatenation, allowing cross-resource collisions

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators and no escaping or length prefixing. Dashboard/folder UIDs can contain underscores, so distinct tuples collide, e.g. (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") produce the same key, as do userUID/action boundary variants. A denial legitimately cached for one resource therefore returns Allowed:false for a different resource the user may actually have access to. Encode the components unambiguously (e.g. hash the tuple or use a separator that cannot appear and length-prefix fields).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing anonymous denials to poison renderer checks

userPermDenialCacheKey is built only from namespace, checkReq.UserUID, action, name and parent, and Check consults it before dispatching on IdentityType. Anonymous subjects (anonymous:0) and renderer subjects (render:0) both parse to UserUID "0", so an anonymous Check for dashboards:read on dash1 that is denied writes a denial entry under UID 0, and a subsequent render:0 Check for the same namespace/action/name/parent hits that entry at line 117 and returns Allowed:false without ever reaching getRendererPermissions, which is supposed to allow renderers to read all dashboards/folders. The same collision applies between user and service-account subjects sharing a UID string. The key must include the identity type (or the denial cache must not be applied to renderer/anonymous identities).

List still trusts stale cached permissions with no freshness fallback

Unlike Check, which now falls back to getIdentityPermissions when cached permissions do not allow the requested resource, List at line 180 returns whatever getCachedIdentityPermissions returns (permissionCacheUsage hit) and never re-queries the DB. After a user creates or is granted a dashboard/folder, List - the API used to fetch visible resources - will omit the new resource until permCache expires (30s), so the PR's goal of letting creators fetch newly created dashboards/folders is not achieved for listing even though single-resource Check now works.

Negative caching reintroduces stale denials for newly granted/created resources

After the new DB re-query, any !allowed result is cached in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s) and subsequent Checks short-circuit at line 117 without re-querying. If a user (or UI) checks a dashboard/folder before its permission row exists or before an admin grants access, and the grant/creation then happens, the creator/grantee is still denied for up to 30s - the exact stale-denial symptom this PR aims to fix for newly created dashboards/folders. It is also set when checkPermission failed only because the folder tree came from the still-cached folderCache (buildFolderTree is not refreshed on the DB fallback), so a stale tree produces a persistent 30s denial even after permissions are re-fetched.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Empty-expression filter runs before interpolation, not after

The targets are filtered with .filter((query) => query.expr) before .map(applyTemplateVariables). A target whose expression is only a template variable, e.g. expr='$myQuery', passes the filter, but if the variable interpolates to an empty string the resulting empty query is no longer filtered out; it is then classified by isLogsQuery(''), grouped, and sent to the backend in a sub-request instead of being ignored like other empty queries.
