organization_context.member may be None

enable_advanced is computed as request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access. For non-superuser requests where the organization context has no member (e.g. superuser-less API/token contexts that reach this endpoint, or members not yet resolved), evaluating .has_global_access on None raises AttributeError and 500s a previously working endpoint; the check is evaluated on every request, not only when optimized_pagination=true, because Python evaluates the right-hand side regardless of use_optimized's value only gated by the boolean expression order — actually enable_advanced is always computed before the if, so all non-superuser requests without a member regress.

Insert-time eviction silently discards earliest-ending spans from segments

Once a merged set exceeds a hardcoded 1000 members, zpopmin removes the lowest-scored members, where the score is now end_timestamp_precise. This silently deletes arbitrary child spans (those ending earliest) from a segment that will later be flushed as if complete, with no metric, log, or segment-too-large outcome as the previous flush-time check produced. It corrupts segment data rather than rejecting/skipping oversized segments, and the hardcoded 1000 also ignores SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001) and any configured value.

SET-to-ZSET conversion breaks in-flight Redis segments during deployment

Existing span-buf:s:* keys in Redis are regular sets created by SADD. The new code unconditionally issues ZADD in process_spans, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN in add-buffer.lua, and ZSCAN in _load_segment_data against those same key names. Redis returns WRONGTYPE for these commands on set-typed keys, so during rollout every trace with an unflushed segment (up to redis_ttl=3600s old) errors in the consumer pipeline instead of being flushed; there is no key versioning, type check, or migration/drain step.

Flush-time max_segment_spans guard removed with no equivalent for non-Lua growth

_load_segment_data no longer enforces max_segment_spans (the metric/log/skip branch was deleted). The only remaining cap is the Lua insert path, which does not cover segments already stored as sets, keys built by the initial batched ZADD before per-span Lua runs interleaved with other batches, or future writers. Oversized segments can now be loaded and produced downstream unbounded by span count, reintroducing the memory/downstream-size risk the guard existed for.

Redirect chain traversal cut from 10000 to 1000 breaks deep segment trees

The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects to find the canonical set for a span now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000, and the comment explaining that deeper trees may not join correctly was removed. Segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects will resolve set_span_id to an intermediate span, so spans are split into multiple segments (flushed separately with wrong segment_id/is_segment attribution) — a silent correctness regression for deep traces that previously worked.

Required end_timestamp_precise turns malformed/legacy spans into poison pills

process_batch now does val['end_timestamp_precise'] with direct indexing for every message. Any span payload lacking that field (older producers, partial/relay variants the previous code tolerated since it never read the field) raises KeyError inside the batch function, failing the whole batch and causing redelivery of the same poison message indefinitely. The new Span field in buffer.py is also a required positional-or-keyword argument added before the defaulted is_segment_span, breaking any other Span(...) construction sites that don't pass it.

sum(sample_weight) undercounts events whose sample_weight is NULL

The aggregate is sum(sample_weight) with no coalesce/fallback. Events stored before client error sampling was populated, or events without a sample rate, can have NULL sample_weight; ClickHouse sum ignores NULLs, so those events contribute 0 instead of 1. Once any allowlisted project is queried, historical/unsampled errors silently disappear from count() results instead of counting with weight 1 (e.g. sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))).

Substring check treats negated/non-error queries as error-focused

_is_error_focused_query returns True whenever the raw query text contains 'event.type:error', including '!event.type:error' (explicitly excluding errors), quoted/tag values containing that text, or a broader OR query that also includes transactions. For Discover this incorrectly rewrites count() to sum(sample_weight) for transaction/non-error results, yielding wrong totals or queries against rows without meaningful sample_weight. The parsed query conditions, not a substring search, need to establish that results are errors only.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public user-callable function

Unlike the internal count helpers around it, the new SnQLFunction is not marked private=True. Any user can therefore send yAxis=upsampled_count() directly on any Discover query/project, bypassing the endpoint's all-projects-allowlisted and error-only checks. On transaction queries this can fail on sample_weight or return misleading weighted counts; the function should be private so only the server-side rewrite can invoke it.

Cache key compresses project IDs into a single hash value

Eligibility is cached under hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))) rather than the project IDs themselves. Different project sets whose tuple hash collides share one cached allowlist verdict for 60s, so a non-allowlisted set can be treated as allowlisted (or vice versa) and counts are silently weighted/unweighted incorrectly. invalidate_upsampling_cache repeats the same scheme and cannot disambiguate. Build the key from the joined sorted IDs instead of a lossy hash.

`'<%= request.referer %>'` inserts the Referer header into a single-quoted JS string with no JavaScript/HTML escaping. A referer containing a quote or `</script>` breaks out of the string/script context and executes attacker JS in the Discourse origin inside the embed iframe. Additionally, postMessage's targetOrigin must be a serialized origin (scheme/host/port), not a full URL with a path; passing the full referer will cause browsers to drop the resize message, so legitimate resizing also fails.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the golden issue: using the full referrer URL instead of an origin as postMessage's targetOrigin causes resize messages to be dropped. Its additional injection concern does not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
import mutates caller's contents string and interpolates unescaped URL into HTML

`contents << "...#{url}..."` mutates the string passed by the caller (raising FrozenError for frozen literals and corrupting reused strings, e.g. feed item content reused on retry), and the URL is interpolated unescaped into a single-quoted href attribute. A URL containing a quote can break out of the attribute and inject markup into the raw-HTML post. Duplicate the contents string first and HTML-escape/attribute-escape the URL when building the imported-from link.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unescaped URL interpolation and resulting XSS vulnerability. However, it discusses string mutation and FrozenError rather than the golden comment's nil-contents NoMethodError, so it matches the XSS concern but not the nil-handling concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed crashes on feed items without content and one bad item aborts the whole import

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` raises NoMethodError when an RSS/Atom item has no content element (common for summary-only feeds; SimpleRSS may return nil or a different field such as description/summary). Because there is no per-item rescue, the exception aborts poll_feed mid-loop, so all remaining items are never imported and the hourly job fails on every run for such a feed. Guard nil content (fall back to description/summary) and isolate failures per item.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that i.content can be nil for feed items, causing i.content.scrub to raise an exception, and recommend falling back to description. The candidate's additional discussion of import failure does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped referer interpolated into JavaScript and used as postMessage targetOrigin

`'<%= request.referer %>'` inserts the Referer header into a single-quoted JS string with no JavaScript/HTML escaping. A referer containing a quote or `</script>` breaks out of the string/script context and executes attacker JS in the Discourse origin inside the embed iframe. Additionally, postMessage's targetOrigin must be a serialized origin (scheme/host/port), not a full URL with a path; passing the full referer will cause browsers to drop the resize message, so legitimate resizing also fails.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying XSS issue: request.referer is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, allowing malicious header content to execute scripts. The additional postMessage concern does not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Raw-HTML posts bypass all sanitization, enabling stored XSS from feeds/remote pages

Post#cook returns `raw` verbatim when cook_method is raw_html, and TopicEmbed.import creates such posts from untrusted RSS/Atom content (Jobs::PollFeed) and arbitrary remote-page content extracted by Readability (TopicEmbed.import_remote). Neither path sanitizes script tags, event-handler attributes, or javascript: URLs before storage, and views output post.cooked (e.g. embed/best.html.erb uses `raw post.cooked`, and normal topic views trust cooked HTML). A malicious or compromised feed/page on the embeddable host therefore stores active HTML/JS that executes in the Discourse origin for every reader, not only in the embed iframe.

import_remote fetches arbitrary URLs server-side with open() and no timeout/validation

TopicEmbed.import_remote does `open(url).read` on a URL ultimately derived from the user-supplied embed_url parameter (EmbedController -> Jobs::RetrieveTopic -> TopicRetriever). TopicRetriever only compares URI host to embeddable_host; there is no timeout, size limit, scheme validation inside import itself, or protection against redirects to internal addresses (open-uri follows redirects). A URL on the allowed host that redirects to an internal/metadata endpoint, or a slow/huge response, can be used for SSRF or to tie up Sidekiq workers. Validate the final URL, set open/read timeouts, and cap response size.

Spec expects TopicRetriever in controller but implementation enqueues Jobs::RetrieveTopic

The 'tells the topic retriever to work' example stubs/expects TopicRetriever.new and retriever.retrieve, but EmbedController#best at app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:15 instead calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...). TopicRetriever is never referenced by the controller, so this expectation fails (Jobs.enqueue is not stubbed and may enqueue a real job). The test as shipped does not pass against the implementation and does not verify the RetrieveTopic job arguments; update it to expect Jobs.enqueue with user_id/embed_url.

Disqus import silently drops the --category option and now requires fetching each thread URL

The change removes the documented `method_option :category` (breaking existing invocations that pass -c, which Thor will now reject/ignore) and replaces local PostCreator creation with TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], ...), which performs a live HTTP fetch of each Disqus thread link. If a link is dead, redirects, or the site is offline, post becomes nil and all comments for that thread are silently skipped, whereas previously the topic was created locally from the export data. Preserve category support or document its removal, and fall back to creating the topic from export data when the remote fetch fails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second downsize definition silently overrides the existing width/height API

Lines 145-151 define OptimizedImage.downsize twice: first as downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) and then as downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}). In Ruby the second definition replaces the first, so any existing caller using the four-argument width/height form will now either raise ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments) or have its max_width value interpreted as a complete dimensions string. This is an API/contract break for other thumbnail/downsize callers, not just the new uploads-controller caller.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the duplicate downsize definitions and explain that the dimensions-string version overrides the separate width/height version, breaking existing callers of the original API.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10 MB client limit ignores configured image and attachment limits

validateUploadedFile previously used Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], which distinguishes images from attachments and respects admin configuration; it now always allows 10 * 1024 KB. If an admin configures a lower limit, the client will accept and upload files the server then rejects (the server-side downsizing only applies to images, so oversized attachments are uploaded in full just to fail), and if an admin configures a higher limit, the client incorrectly blocks valid uploads. The hardcoded value also makes the file_too_large message report 10240 KB regardless of the actual configured limit.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: hardcoding the client upload limit to 10 * 1024 KB ignores the configured per-type SiteSettings limits, potentially diverging from server-side limits. The candidate matches the underlying issue even though it does not explicitly mention the 413 handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Percentage downsizing is incompatible with the animated-GIF instructions

The new upload path passes dimensions "80%" with allow_animation taken from SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails. When that setting is true and the file is a GIF, optimize() dispatches to downsize_instructions_animated, which forwards "80%" to resize_instructions_animated as the argument to gifsicle's --resize-fit. --resize-fit expects a WxH geometry, not a percentage scale (gifsicle uses a different option for scaling), so animated GIF downsizing will fail; convert_with returns false, the controller ignores that result, retries the same failing command up to five times, and then proceeds with the still-oversized file.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: passing "80%" for animated GIF downsizing when allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled sends a percentage to gifsicle --resize-fit, which expects WxH geometry, causing downsizing to fail. The candidate adds details about retries and ignored failure without changing the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize result is ignored and the loop neither guarantees nor verifies the size limit

The while loop at lines 66-69 calls OptimizedImage.downsize up to five times but discards its boolean return value and performs no check after the loop. If conversion fails, produces a larger file (possible when re-encoding formats such as PNG without a quality/compression change in downsize_instructions), or five 80% reductions are still not enough to get under SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb, create_upload silently continues to Upload.create_for with an oversized/corrupt intermediate file. The feature therefore either fails later with the old size error after expensive retries or stores an upload that does not satisfy the stated invariant.

In-place conversion uses the same path for input and output

OptimizedImage.downsize is called with tempfile.path as both source and destination. The downsize instructions run ImageMagick `convert <file>[0] ... <file>` (and for animated images gifsicle with --output set to the input file), rather than converting to a separate temporary file and atomically replacing the original only on success. Tools that truncate/create the output before fully consuming the input, or that fail part-way, can leave the user's only uploaded copy truncated or corrupted; because the return value is ignored and ensure only closes the tempfile, the corrupted file is then passed to Upload.create_for instead of preserving the original upload.

413 error handler reports a fabricated 10 MB maximum

In displayErrorForUpload's 413 branch, the message previously used Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb and now always interpolates 10 * 1024 KB as max_size_kb. A 413 is generated by the web server/proxy limit, which is unrelated to this constant, so users will be told the limit is 10 MB even when the proxy or site setting allows far less or more, sending them to retry with files that will continue to fail.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser row

TopicUser.find_by can return nil for a logged-in user who has never visited, posted in, or otherwise interacted with the topic (for example, opening the unsubscribe URL directly or after the row was removed). The next line calls tu.notification_level on nil, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500 instead of unsubscribing. The action should create/update the record through the existing TopicUser.change mechanism (as set_notifications does) so a missing row is created with the muted/regular level.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same nil dereference: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil, and calling notification_level on it crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
State-changing unsubscribe is performed by a plain GET request

The new server route is GET t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe and this action immediately mutates notification_level and saves it. Email security scanners, link prefetchers, browser pre-rendering, or a third party tricking a logged-in user into loading the URL (CSRF via GET, which Rails forgery protection does not cover) will unsubscribe/mute the user without any intentional click or confirmation. The GET should only render a confirmation page and the mutation should require a non-GET request, as the Ember notification dropdown already can perform.

Direct TopicUser save bypasses notification-change bookkeeping and leaves stale state

Mutating tu.notification_level and calling tu.save! bypasses TopicUser.change, which is the established path used by set_notifications: it stamps notifications_changed_at, sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed, runs observe_after_save_callbacks_for, and publishes a MessageBus /topic/:id notification_level_change event. Because @topic_view was also built before the mutation, the rendered/serialized response and any already-open client can keep showing the old watching/tracking level even though the database changed, and downstream observers never learn of the change. Use TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...) instead.

topicUnsubscribe route is shadowed by topic.fromParamsNear

The topic resource defined just above already has a child route fromParamsNear with path '/:nearPost', i.e. /t/:slug/:id/:nearPost, which matches the literal segment 'unsubscribe'. Ember's router recognises routes in definition order, so /t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe is matched as the normal topic page with nearPost='unsubscribe' before the later top-level topicUnsubscribe route is considered; the unsubscribe template/controller therefore never renders on a full page load or transition. The unsubscribe route needs to be defined so it wins recognition over the :nearPost wildcard (or handled inside the topic route).

Emails with add_unsubscribe_link but no topic unsubscribe_url now raise

The server locale string unsubscribe_link now interpolates %{unsubscribe_url}, and both body (line 90) and html_part (line 67) call I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args) whenever add_unsubscribe_link is true. MessageBuilder is generic: any caller that sets add_unsubscribe_link without also passing unsubscribe_url (previously valid, and the behaviour the existing specs exercised before they were edited to pass a URL) will now raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument and fail to deliver the email instead of falling back to the plain user-preferences unsubscribe text. The per-topic sentence should only be appended when unsubscribe_url is present.

No test covers the new unsubscribe behaviour end-to-end

The only spec change passes unsubscribe_url into an existing builder fixture but adds no assertion that the topic unsubscribe URL appears in the text body or HTML part, and there are no controller specs for TopicsController#unsubscribe at all (level transitions watching/tracking->regular and regular->muted, missing TopicUser row, wrong slug redirect, JSON vs HTML). The core state-transition logic of this feature can regress or crash without any test failing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed invocation is macOS-only and the script exits 0 on failure

`sed -i '' -E ...` uses BSD/macOS syntax; on GNU/Linux sed treats '' as an input file and fails, so GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never updated while the script continues and prints success. Additionally the failure paths at lines 49 and 58 call cleanup(), which unconditionally `exit 0`, masking rate-limit and tunnel-start failures. Use a portable in-place edit (or OS detection) and exit non-zero on the error paths.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same portability bug: BSD/macOS `sed -i ''` syntax fails on GNU/Linux. The additional concern about masked failures does not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization failure is thrown as a generic Error instead of a TRPCError

When the credential does not belong to the session user the handler throws `new Error('Credential not found or access denied')`. In tRPC this surfaces as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) rather than a NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN client error, so clients and monitoring treat a routine bad/foreign credentialId as a server failure. Throw a TRPCError with an appropriate code instead, as other viewer handlers do.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that throwing a generic Error for an authentication or authorization failure causes tRPC to return a 500 instead of an appropriate structured TRPCError, such as FORBIDDEN.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting cache does not invalidate connectedCalendars query

deleteCacheMutation only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess callback. Unlike disconnectMutation (lines 61-64) it never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars, and in SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper onChanged is props.onChanged which may be undefined. After a successful deletion the cached query still contains the old cacheUpdatedAt, so the dropdown continues to show 'Cache Status / Delete cached data' as if the cache still exists until a manual refetch/remount.

Cache status includes expired cache entries that will never be served

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups all CalendarCache rows for the credentials without filtering expiresAt. getCachedAvailability treats rows with expiresAt < now as a cache miss, so connectedCalendars can report cacheUpdatedAt and the UI can offer 'Delete cached data' for a cache that is already expired/dead. The status query should only consider unexpired rows (expiresAt >= now), matching the read path.

dev:cron now depends on unpinned npx-fetched tsx that is not a declared dependency

The script was changed from ts-node (a declared devDependency, line 196) to `npx tsx`, but tsx is not declared anywhere in this package's dependencies. Running dev:cron therefore requires a network fetch of an unpinned package on first use, fails offline/in locked-down installs, and is a supply-chain/reproducibility regression unrelated to the calendar-cache feature. Add tsx as a devDependency (pinned by the lockfile) or keep ts-node.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check rejects slots covered by any non-first range and uses wrong end/day

This block returns unavailable if ANY workingHour entry for that weekday does not contain the slot (find on start<startTime||end>endTime), instead of checking whether NO entry contains it. Users with split/multiple ranges on the same day will lose slots covered by a later range. Additionally end at line 142 is copied from slotStartTime rather than slotEndTime, so a slot starting inside working hours but ending after endTime passes, and both day()/hour() are taken from the UTC slot time while WorkingHours days/startTime/endTime are expressed in the organizer's schedule timezone, so non-UTC hosts are compared on the wrong day and hour.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that the end time is copied from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, matching the golden issue. The additional concerns do not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Empty date-override comparison uses object identity and never matches

dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...) compares two distinct Dayjs objects with ===, which is always false, so the intended zero-length override (whole day unavailable) branch is dead. A slot that straddles the equal start/end instant then falls through both boundary checks, sets dateOverrideExist, and is returned as available instead of unavailable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: using === to compare distinct Dayjs objects checks reference identity rather than date values, making the equality condition always false. The candidate's additional discussion of consequences does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots inside a date override bypass busy-time checks

When a slot is on a date-override day and inside the override window, the find callback returns nothing, dateOverrideExist is true, and checkIfIsAvailable returns true at line 134 without reaching the busy.every() check at the bottom. A fixed or round-robin host can therefore be shown/booked during a date-override slot even when they have an accepted Cal booking or a busy calendar event overlapping that slot.

Date override shifted across midnight is truncated/wrong-day

startTime/endTime are derived only from hour()*60+minute() after adding the invitee-organizer offset. If the offset pushes the override across midnight (common when organizer and invitee are on opposite sides of the date line), endTime can become smaller than startTime or both wrap to the next day's clock time while activeOverrides still matched the override against the unshifted invitee day at line 207. buildSlots discards start>=end boundaries, so such overrides disappear or appear on the wrong day.

No test for the round-robin fixed-host date-override fix

The PR description claims fixed hosts' date overrides are now honoured for round-robin events, but the only added test re-queries the existing personal-event date-override scenario in Asia/Dhaka and expects identical UTC slots. There is no scenario with schedulingType ROUND_ROBIN, a fixed host with an override, and a loose host, nor a case where the fixed host's calendar/booking conflicts inside the override, so the new checkIfIsAvailable filtering for fixed/loose hosts is untested and the busy-bypass regression above would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry increment is a stale read-modify-write, not atomic

Both increments (lines 184 and 195) write `reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value snapshotted by the findMany at the start of the run. If two cron invocations overlap, both read retryCount 0 and both write 1, so the counter never exceeds 1, the `retryCount > 1` deletion never triggers, and failing reminders are retried forever (and may also double-schedule with Twilio). Using Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }` avoids the lost update.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same stale read-modify-write bug in retryCount updates, which can lose increments during concurrent runs, and recommend Prisma's atomic increment for both update locations.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry-count deletion clause is not scoped to SMS reminders

The original deleteMany was scoped to `method: SMS`; in the new OR the second branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no method (or scheduled/date) constraint, so it deletes WorkflowReminder rows of any method (EMAIL/WHATSAPP share this table per WorkflowMethods) once their retryCount exceeds 1, even if they are future-dated and not this SMS cron's responsibility. Scoping it to SMS (like the first branch) keeps this handler from deleting other channels' reminders.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the retryCount > 1 deletion branch lacks an SMS method filter, causing non-SMS workflow reminders such as Email and WhatsApp to be deleted.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders with no message or recipient are never counted or deleted

The retry increment only runs when twilio.scheduleSMS returns null or throws. If message is empty/null or sendTo is falsy, the `if (message?.length && ... && sendTo)` block is skipped entirely: the reminder stays unscheduled with retryCount 0, is re-fetched on every cron run, and the new `retryCount > 1` cleanup never fires. This leaves the exact infinite-rescheduling loop the PR aims to fix in place for missing/invalid phone numbers or empty templates (and similarly for the `continue` at lines 68-70 when workflowStep/booking is missing, which also never increments).

Unhandled update inside catch can abort the whole cron run

The catch block now awaits `prisma.workflowReminder.update` without its own error handling. If that update fails (e.g. P2025 because the reminder was deleted by the concurrent cleanup/another run, or a transient DB error), the exception propagates out of the per-reminder try/catch, aborting the loop so all remaining unscheduled reminders are skipped and the handler returns 500 instead of `SMS scheduled`. Previously the catch only logged. The increment should be wrapped so a failure to record a retry does not break processing of the other reminders.

Unparenthesized OR authorization conditions leak when composed with other WHERE clauses

getBaseConditions returns authConditions directly when there are no filter conditions (line 75), and for org/team scopes that condition is built as `(A) OR (B)` without outer parentheses (lines 171-174 and 204-207). A caller composing it as `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND <date/status condition>` gets `(A) OR (B) AND <condition>` because AND binds tighter than OR in SQL, so the first authorization branch ignores the caller's additional condition. The old Prisma WhereInput guaranteed this OR was grouped. The returned fragment should be wrapped, e.g. Prisma.sql`(${authConditions})`, so composition is safe.

Public findMany method is removed without migrating any call sites

This change deletes InsightsBookingService.findMany, which previously ran bookingTimeStatusDenormalized.findMany with the authorization and filter conditions merged into the caller's where clause, and replaces it with getBaseConditions that only returns a SQL fragment. No caller in this PR is updated to issue its own $queryRaw query, so any existing consumer of findMany breaks (TypeScript compile error / runtime 'findMany is not a function'), and former consumers that passed select/orderBy/etc. lose that behavior entirely. Call sites must be migrated in the same PR or findMany retained on top of the new conditions.

ANY(array) authorization branches are never executed against the database

The only test that executes SQL against Postgres is the user-scope test at lines 480-491, which exercises `userId = $1 AND teamId IS NULL`. The org and team scopes, which rely on `"teamId" = ANY(${numberArray})` and `"userId" = ANY(${numberArray})` parameter binding, are only asserted by Prisma.Sql object equality (lines 295-343). Object equality cannot detect a Postgres runtime failure or wrong typing when Prisma binds a JavaScript number array to ANY(...), so the highest-risk raw-SQL authorization paths could fail at query time while all tests pass. Add $queryRaw executions for org and team scopes.

Caching tests were deleted while the caching behavior remains

The PR removes the 'Caching' describe block that verified repeated getAuthorizationConditions()/getFilterConditions() calls return the cached result, but insightsBooking.ts still implements cachedAuthConditions/cachedFilterConditions (lines 84-95). There is now no coverage guarding that cache against regressions (e.g. returning stale or uncached conditions), and the deletion is unrelated to the Prisma.sql conversion since the same assertions work with SQL fragments.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dummy refresh_token overwrites the real refresh token

When the (stripped) parsed response has no refresh_token, this sets refresh_token to the literal string "refresh_token". Callers persist that value: Zoom assigns key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token and Office365 spreads tokenResponse.data into the stored credential. With credential sharing enabled the real refresh token in the database is irreversibly replaced by the placeholder, so disabling sharing later or falling back to the provider leaves the credential permanently unrefreshable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: a missing refresh_token in the parsed OAuth response is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token", corrupting the stored token and breaking subsequent refreshes. The candidate adds persistence details but describes the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Minimum token schema strips expiry and provider-specific fields

minimumTokenResponseSchema only declares access_token plus computed keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()], which are literal object-string keys, not wildcards. Zod strips unknown keys by default, so when sharing is enabled expires_in/expiry_date, scope, token_type, instance_url and other fields required by callers are dropped from .data. The isinstance check therefore skips process.kill() for a hung flusher, after which _create_process_for_shards starts a replacement for the same shards. The hung and replacement processes can then concurrently flush the same Redis shards, racing flush/done_flush and potentially producing duplicate segments or interfering with each other's in-progress flushes.

A direct flusher_processes=0 via the factory is instead silently converted by `max_processes or len(...)` to one process per shard, the opposite of the requested limit. The threaded produce_to_pipe path with multiple shards sharing processes, per-process restart/health bookkeeping, and the spawn-process path used in production are all unexercised, so regressions that drop or duplicate segments when shards share a flusher (or when a flusher restarts) would pass CI.

false_positives.candidate:
Shutdown abandons queued work items

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True for every worker before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() only checks `while not self.shutdown` at the top of its loop, so a worker that finishes its current item exits immediately even if its queue still contains pending items, and a worker blocked in get() that returns an item may process at most one more. The remaining queued items are therefore never processed and their offsets never complete, contrary to the immediate=False drain semantics. On consumer shutdown/rebalance those messages must be redelivered (or are lost if later code marks them complete), defeating the claimed graceful shutdown.

Final offsets are never committed on close and closed pool is reused after rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown(), so any items drained/completed during pool shutdown are completed after the last _commit_loop iteration and are never passed to commit_function. Worse, the queue_pool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory and the same pool is passed to every strategy from create_with_partitions(); close() shuts its queues down irreversibly (queue.shutdown()), so after an Arroyo partition rebalance/revocation the factory creates a new strategy backed by a dead pool. Subsequent FixedQueuePool.submit() puts raise queue.ShutDown, which SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches and then add_offset+complete_offset, causing offsets to be committed without the results ever being processed.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize and submit() does an unconditional put(). The class/strategy docstrings claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing ever blocks or rejects: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() is called by Arroyo for every polled message and will enqueue indefinitely if one subscription/queue is slow, growing memory unboundedly, holding WorkItem/message references, and building a huge outstanding-offset window that can stall commits and trigger max.poll.interval rebalances. A bounded queue (with blocking or Arroyo-appropriate rejection) is required.

OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition revocation

OffsetTracker keeps all_offsets/outstanding/last_committed/partition_locks forever and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy exposes no revocation/flush hook to clear a partition. If a partition is revoked and later reassigned (possibly at an offset <= the previously recorded last_committed, e.g. after a rebalance or offset reset), get_committable_offsets() starts at last_committed+1 and can never emit a commit until processing passes the stale high-water mark, so processed results go uncommitted and are redelivered; removed partitions also leak sets/locks for the life of the factory-owned pool.

Commit scan is O(offset window) every second

get_committable_offsets() runs every 1s in _commit_loop and, per partition, iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)`, i.e. over the entire uncommitted offset window, allocating/scanning proportionally to backlog size. Combined with the unbounded queues, a large backlog (exactly the slow-item scenario this mode targets) makes each commit tick O(window) per partition and can consume a full thread/CPU while commits fall further behind. Tracking only the contiguous head (e.g. sorted outstanding minimum) would be O(1)/O(log n).

Group-to-queue assignment uses randomized hash()

get_queue_for_group() uses Python's built-in hash() on a str, which is randomized per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, despite the docstring calling it 'consistent hashing'. The mapping differs across consumer processes/restarts, so the same subscription is not consistently assigned as documented and distribution cannot be reasoned about or reproduced in tests/operations; within a fleet this also gives no stable sharding guarantee. Use a stable digest (e.g. hashlib/md5 already used elsewhere for grouping) modulo num_queues.

Eligibility is cached under hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))) rather than the project IDs themselves. Different project sets whose tuple hash collides share one cached allowlist verdict for 60s, so a non-allowlisted set can be treated as allowlisted (or vice versa) and counts are silently weighted/unweighted incorrectly. invalidate_upsampling_cache repeats the same scheme and cannot disambiguate. Build the key from the joined sorted IDs instead of a lossy hash.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))) cache key and suggest a deterministic serialization of the joined IDs instead. The golden's concern is non-determinism across processes due to hash randomization. The candidate's concern is hash collisions. Integer tuple hashes are actually deterministic across processes, so the golden's rationale is debatable, but the two still diverge on the root cause. They share the code location and the fix but not the core reasoning, so this is a partial match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset

_get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset, which get_event_stats_factory may replace (e.g. dashboard discover-split passes split_dataset=discover or the original scoped dataset), but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` instead. The transform decision therefore does not describe the dataset actually queried: split/error queries can miss upsampling and transaction-like split queries can be transformed based on the wrong dataset, producing wrong counts or invalid sample_weight queries.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The upsampling eligibility check uses the outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`. In dashboard split paths this makes the upsampling decision wrong.

false_positives.candidate:
upsampled_count is enabled for the errors dataset but only registered in Discover

_should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True unconditionally for sentry.snuba.errors, so count() is rewritten to upsampled_count() for dataset=errors requests. The new SnQLFunction is only added to Discover's function_converter in src/sentry/search/events/datasets/discover.py; the errors dataset has its own function converter and does not gain this function from that change. Errors-dataset timeseries requests for allowlisted projects will fail function resolution instead of returning upsampled counts.

sum(sample_weight) undercounts events whose sample_weight is NULL

The aggregate is sum(sample_weight) with no coalesce/fallback. Events stored before client error sampling was populated, or events without a sample rate, can have NULL sample_weight; ClickHouse sum ignores NULLs, so those events contribute 0 instead of 1. Once any allowlisted project is queried, historical/unsampled errors silently disappear from count() results instead of counting with weight 1 (e.g. sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))).

Substring check treats negated/non-error queries as error-focused

_is_error_focused_query returns True whenever the raw query text contains 'event.type:error', including '!event.type:error' (explicitly excluding errors), quoted/tag values containing that text, or a broader OR query that also includes transactions. For Discover this incorrectly rewrites count() to sum(sample_weight) for transaction/non-error results, yielding wrong totals or queries against rows without meaningful sample_weight. The parsed query conditions, not a substring search, need to establish that results are errors only.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public user-callable function

Unlike the internal count helpers around it, the new SnQLFunction is not marked private=True. Any user can therefore send yAxis=upsampled_count() directly on any Discover query/project, bypassing the endpoint's all-projects-allowlisted and error-only checks. On transaction queries this can fail on sample_weight or return misleading weighted counts; the function should be private so only the server-side rewrite can invoke it.

Accidental gitlink file added to the repository root

The PR adds a new root entry 'sentry-repo' containing 'Subproject commit a5d2909...', i.e. an accidental nested-repo gitlink rather than application code. Merging it creates a stray submodule-like entry without .gitmodules metadata, which breaks/clutters checkouts and tooling; it should be removed from the change.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key uses ambiguous underscore concatenation, allowing cross-resource collisions

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators and no escaping or length prefixing. Dashboard/folder UIDs can contain underscores, so distinct tuples collide, e.g. (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") produce the same key, as do userUID/action boundary variants. A denial legitimately cached for one resource therefore returns Allowed:false for a different resource the user may actually have access to. Encode the components unambiguously (e.g. hash the tuple or use a separator that cannot appear and length-prefix fields).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same flaw. userPermDenialCacheKey joins its fields with underscores, which makes keys ambiguous when a field itself contains underscores. That leads to collisions and incorrect denial cache hits that affect user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing anonymous denials to poison renderer checks

userPermDenialCacheKey is built only from namespace, checkReq.UserUID, action, name and parent, and Check consults it before dispatching on IdentityType. Anonymous subjects (anonymous:0) and renderer subjects (render:0) both parse to UserUID "0", so an anonymous Check for dashboards:read on dash1 that is denied writes a denial entry under UID 0, and a subsequent render:0 Check for the same namespace/action/name/parent hits that entry at line 117 and returns Allowed:false without ever reaching getRendererPermissions, which is supposed to allow renderers to read all dashboards/folders. The same collision applies between user and service-account subjects sharing a UID string. The key must include the identity type (or the denial cache must not be applied to renderer/anonymous identities).

Negative caching reintroduces stale denials for newly granted/created resources

After the new DB re-query, any !allowed result is cached in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s) and subsequent Checks short-circuit at line 117 without re-querying. If a user (or UI) checks a dashboard/folder before its permission row exists or before an admin grants access, and the grant/creation then happens, the creator/grantee is still denied for up to 30s - the exact stale-denial symptom this PR aims to fix for newly created dashboards/folders. It is also set when checkPermission failed only because the folder tree came from the still-cached folderCache (buildFolderTree is not refreshed on the DB fallback), so a stale tree produces a persistent 30s denial even after permissions are re-fetched.

List still trusts stale cached permissions with no freshness fallback

Unlike Check, which now falls back to getIdentityPermissions when cached permissions do not allow the requested resource, List at line 180 returns whatever getCachedIdentityPermissions returns (permissionCacheUsage hit) and never re-queries the DB. After a user creates or is granted a dashboard/folder, List - the API used to fetch visible resources - will omit the new resource until permCache expires (30s), so the PR's goal of letting creators fetch newly created dashboards/folders is not achieved for listing even though single-resource Check now works.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:

The explicit SQL-expression rejection was added only to ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery in pkg/expr/reader.go. If TablesList/the stub DB is ever restored or changed, this entry point silently becomes reachable again. This security change adds no test asserting that QueryTypeSQL is rejected when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, nor that the legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is rejected, and it does not update the existing SQL-expression tests that exercise NewSQLCommand/TablesList/Execute (which now always fail via the stub DB). Without a regression test, a future refactor of enableSqlExpressions or the stub DB could re-enable the DuckDB-backed RCE/LFI surface unnoticed, and the current test suite is left failing or must be silently skipped. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock is acquired without re-checking the cache and is held across file I/O

After acquiring entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock(), GetWebAssets does not check entryPointAssetsCache again before reloading. Concurrent callers that all missed the initial RLock fast path will queue on the write lock and then each sequentially repeat readWebAssetsFromFile (and overwrite the cache) while holding the lock across disk I/O. This serializes cold-start (and every Dev-mode) requests and performs redundant manifest reads instead of letting all but the first caller reuse the newly populated cache; add a double-checked cache test inside the write lock and return the cached value when another goroutine populated it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same flaw: once the write lock is acquired, the cache is never checked again, so goroutines that were waiting for the lock each reload the assets redundantly. This is the missing second check of double-checked locking.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent test covers the race being fixed

The change adds synchronization around the global entryPointAssetsCache but no test exercises concurrent GetWebAssets calls, so a regression (e.g. a future unsynchronized access to the cache) would not be caught even under `go test -race`. Add a test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines in parallel (covering both the cached fast path and the initial load) and run it with the race detector.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

Successful routine cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification

The background cleanup ticker is changed from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1, so all cleanup jobs including the now multi-query annotation cleanup run 10x more often. This is unrelated to the deadlock fix described in the PR, is not mentioned in the description, and increases steady-state database and CPU load on every Grafana instance. The candidate adds context, noting the change is unjustified and unrelated to the PR's deadlock fix, but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite, leaving large batches broken on PostgreSQL

deleteByIDs inlines IDs only when the DB is SQLite and the configured batch size exceeds 999; otherwise it builds one '?' placeholder per ID. PostgreSQL has a 65535 bind-parameter limit (and drivers/DBs have similar limits), so a configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above that limit makes DELETE ... IN (?,...,?) fail with too-many-parameters, whereas the previous single-statement DELETE had no bind parameters and worked for any batch size. The decision is also based on the configured batch size rather than len(ids). Chunk the delete by actual ID count or inline/chunk for all dialects.

SQLite ID inlining builds the IN list quadratically

For SQLite batches over 999, values is rebuilt with fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) for every ID, copying the entire accumulated string each iteration. With the tested batch size of 32767 (and larger allowed configurations) this is O(n^2) copying and allocations on the cleanup path. Build the list with strings.Builder / strconv instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug. The context is built with d.Log instead of the enriched log variable, so the name, kind and method values are lost from the logging context.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Storage failures are recorded as legacy metrics

On Storage.Create error this records `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`, and Update does the same at line 129. Storage failures will inflate legacy error/latency metrics and leave storage metrics missing, misleading the dashboards/alerts used to judge whether mode 3 can be trusted. DeleteCollection's async goroutine at line 166 conversely calls recordStorageDuration for the Legacy.DeleteCollection call, and Delete at line 106 passes `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the kind label on success, creating wrong/high-cardinality series.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says Delete passes `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the kind label for metrics. That is the same issue as the golden comment, even though the candidate also raises other problems.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will usually be cancelled

Create (and the identical patterns in Delete, Update and DeleteCollection) launch `go func()` with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` derived from the incoming request ctx. When the handler returns the created object, the apiserver cancels the request context, so the legacy write racing the response will typically see context.Canceled and never persist. Mode 3's guarantee that legacy is kept in sync as a safety net is therefore broken; the fix is a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) plus timeout) with request-scoped values/logging preserved.

Same object/objInfo shared between returned result and async legacy goroutine

Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create, returns `created` to the caller, and concurrently passes `obj` to Legacy.Create in the goroutine; Update similarly re-uses the same `objInfo` for both stores. Callers/serializers can mutate or read the returned object while the legacy goroutine reads/mutates it (data race), Storage.Create may have set ResourceVersion/UID on obj making a subsequent legacy Create reject it, and UpdatedObjectInfo is not required to be idempotent or safe to evaluate a second time against a different (legacy) old object. The previous implementation used updateWrapper to hand legacy the exact object written to unified storage; dropping that also risks legacy updates computed from stale legacy state with a unified-storage ResourceVersion, causing RV conflicts. Deep-copy/wrap the object for the legacy write before returning.

Async legacy failures are never logged

The legacy goroutines only record a duration metric and discard the returned error (Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection). Previously legacy failures were logged with the object. Combined with the fire-and-forget design, a permanently failing legacy write (e.g. duplicate create, RV conflict, validation) leaves unified and legacy silently diverged with no log line to investigate; at minimum log errObjectSt inside each goroutine.

Mode 3 tests never verify the async legacy write and race its completion

Tests register legacy mock expectations but Create/Update return before the legacy goroutine runs and no test waits for or asserts the legacy call (no AssertCalled / channel / Eventually). The mock.Mock is shared with a goroutine that may execute after the subtest finishes, so expectations can be silently unfulfilled or the stray goroutine can panic/race a later subtest sharing the package-level fixtures. The playlist integration cases in pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go have the same issue: doPlaylistTests immediately asserts the legacy API reflects k8s creates/updates/deletes, which under async mode 3 is inherently racy and will be flaky.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

It can never refresh updated_at, so it stays expired and is rejected until the 61-day cleanup deletes it, even though it should be treated as a (re-)new device subject only to the current count.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to updateDevice returning ErrDeviceLimitReached when 0 rows are affected because the device falls outside the time window. The candidate frames it around expired devices, but it is the same misattribution of 0 rows affected to the limit error.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

Device is cached before DB write, so a rejected device is admitted on retry
